categories.name: Buying
categories.description: Choosing and paying for a car.

posts.title: Seven seats, seven checks before you buy a minivan
posts.excerpt: Sliding doors, third-row legroom and the boring things that decide whether a family car works every day.
posts.content:
Tomás Ortega, our service manager, has a short list for anyone buying a seven-seater, and it starts with the doors. Open and close each sliding door ten times and listen: a smooth rail now is a smooth rail in five years.

Then sit in the third row yourself. If an adult cannot sit there for ten minutes, the seats will be used for luggage and the car is the wrong size.

Last, check where the child seats actually fit. Bring them to the test drive. We are happy to wait while you click them in.

posts.title: Reading the paperwork before you sign
posts.excerpt: A calm walk through the pages that matter: price, finance terms and what the warranty covers.
posts.content:
Priya Raman hands every approved used buyer the same one-page summary before anything is signed: the price, the inspection sheet, the warranty terms and the finance example. If a number on the page is not the number you were told, say so before you pick up the pen.

Our representative example is a 4.9% APR, subject to approval. Your own rate depends on your credit and the term you choose, and we will show you the real figures side by side.

Take the sheet home if you want to. A good deal is still a good deal tomorrow morning.

posts.title: What the 152 points actually cover
posts.excerpt: Brakes, steering, battery, tyres and bodywork: the inspection behind every approved used car.
posts.content:
The 152-point inspection is a printed sheet, and a technician signs every line. It covers brakes, steering and suspension, the battery and charging system, tyres, lights, fluids, bodywork and a road test.

If a car fails a line we fix it or we do not sell the car. You can read the signed sheet for any approved used vehicle on the forecourt.

posts.title: Charging at home: what the first week teaches you
posts.excerpt: A plain-speaking guide to the first seven days with an electric car and a wall charger.
posts.content:
Priya Raman sees the same pattern with every electric hatchback that leaves the lot: the first night is about plugging in, the third night is about working out when the cheap rate starts, and by the end of the week the cable lives in the boot.

Our advice is simple. Charge at home overnight and keep the battery between twenty and eighty percent for daily use. Save the full charge for long trips. Ask your electricity supplier for a time-of-use rate before you buy a wall charger, not after.

Every electric and hybrid car we sell gets the $89 health check at the one-year mark. We read the battery report, test the charge port and update the software, and we show you the numbers on paper.

posts.title: Setting up a calm cabin for the school run
posts.excerpt: Seat height, mirrors and the three things worth fixing before the first drive.
posts.content:
Marcus Bell has a ten-minute routine for every family who buys a car from us. It starts in the driver’s seat, before the key is turned, and it is the reason his customers rarely call to ask where the controls are.

Move the seat until your knees are slightly bent. Set the mirrors so you can only just see the side of your own car. Then sit in each back seat and check that the belts, the latches and the headrests work for the people who will use them.

If anything is stiff, loose or confusing, tell us in the first week. Adjusting a seat rail or a mirror takes five minutes in the service bay and costs nothing on a car we sold you.

posts.title: Five checks before a long drive
posts.excerpt: Tyres, oil, lights, wipers and a full tank: the five-minute list Tomás gives every customer.
posts.content:
Tomás Ortega keeps a laminated card by the service desk with five lines on it. Tyres, oil, lights, wipers, fuel or charge. It takes five minutes and catches most of the problems that end a road trip early.

Check the tyres with a coin or a gauge and look at the sidewalls for bulges. Pull the dipstick on a cold engine. Walk around the car while someone presses the brake pedal and flicks the indicators. Test the wipers on a dry screen, then top up the washer fluid.

If you would like a second pair of eyes, book the $39 state safety inspection at any of our three sites. It takes about forty minutes and you get a printed sheet to take with you.
